content:
Here is the most unsettling sentence I took from a 500-page book:
How sure you feel tells you almost nothing about whether you’re right.
It tells you something else: how smoothly your brain managed to assemble a story. That’s it. Smooth story, high confidence. Messy story, doubt. Truth is not part of the calculation.
That’s the thread running through Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow, the life’s work of a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. I read it so you don’t have to, and kept only the ideas worth stealing. Here are the seven that survived.
1. What you see is all there is Your fast, automatic mind (Kahneman calls it System 1) works with whatever information happens to be lying around, builds the best story it can from it, and hands you the result with a feeling of certainty.
It never says “I’m missing something.” Information it doesn’t have simply doesn’t exist for it. Kahneman’s abbreviation for this is WYSIATI: what you see is all there is.
The experiment that made me wince: people read a legal case, then heard from a lawyer for one side only. They were told they were hearing one side. They could have easily imagined the other lawyer’s pitch. Still, they were more confident in their verdicts than people who heard both sides.
Less information, more confidence. A thin story is easier to make coherent than a rich one.
Steal this: when you feel certain, ask “what would I need to know that I don’t know?” Then go find it before you decide.
2. You rarely answer the question you were asked When a question is hard, your mind quietly swaps it for an easier one and answers that, without telling you.
How happy are you with your life? becomes What’s my mood right now? Will this candidate be a good leader? becomes Does she look like a leader? How popular will the president be in six months? becomes How popular is the president today? You don’t feel the swap. The answer arrives fast and fluent, so it feels like an answer to the real question.
Steal this: for any big judgment, write the actual question down. Then ask: “Is this really what I’m answering?”
3. Confidence is a feeling, not evidence Early in his career, Kahneman helped evaluate soldiers for officer training in the Israeli army. He and his colleagues watched candidates tackle an obstacle course and felt they could see each man’s true character. Then every few months they’d get feedback: their predictions were barely better than guessing.
It changed nothing. The next batch arrived, they watched them haul a log over a wall, and the certainty came right back, as vivid as before.
He named it the illusion of validity: you can know, as a statistic, that your judgments are poor, and still feel that this specific judgment is solid. Like the Müller-Lyer lines, knowing the trick doesn’t make it go away.
Steal this: high confidence from someone (including you) mostly proves they’ve told themselves a coherent story. Treat admitted uncertainty as the more informative signal.
4. A dumb formula beats the smart expert Paul Meehl dared to compare trained clinicians against simple statistical rules. The rules won, and kept winning. After roughly 200 studies, about 60% show the algorithm clearly more accurate, and the rest are ties. Predicting parole violations, business success, cancer survival, college grades. Kahneman notes that no exception has been convincingly documented.
Why do experts lose?
They try to be clever and combine many factors, and complexity usually hurts. They are wildly inconsistent. Experienced radiologists contradict their own reading of the same X-ray about 20% of the time. An economist built a three-variable weather formula that predicts the future price of Bordeaux wine better than the tasters do. And the best-known success story of all is the Apgar score: five quick checks, scored 0 to 2, that replaced gut feel in delivery rooms and, in Kahneman’s telling, has saved the lives of hundreds of thousands of infants.
Even a back-of-the-envelope formula with equal weights often competes with fancy statistics. One of Kahneman’s favorite examples: predict a marriage with how often you make love minus how often you quarrel.
Steal this: for hiring, investing, prioritizing, anything repeated, pick 4 to 6 relevant criteria, score each one separately, add them up, and let the total decide. Use your gut to collect the scores, not to overrule the sum.
5. The test for when to trust intuition Kahneman isn’t saying all intuition is garbage. He spent years arguing with Gary Klein, who studied firefighters that sensed a floor was about to collapse. They finally agreed on a two-part test. Trust an expert’s gut only if:
The environment is regular enough to be predictable, and They’ve had long practice with fast, clear feedback. Chess players, nurses, firefighters, anesthesiologists pass. Stock pickers and long-range political pundits fail, because their world offers no stable patterns to learn. Some environments are worse than useless: Kahneman retells the story of a doctor who “predicted” typhoid in patients. He was accurate, because he was spreading it himself with unwashed hands.
And the line I keep repeating to myself: don’t trust anyone, yourself included, to tell you how much to trust their judgment. Judge the environment and the feedback loop, not the confidence.
Steal this: before you defer to an expert (or to your own hunch), ask two questions. Is this a world with stable patterns? Did this person get quick, honest feedback in it?
6. Your plan is a best-case fantasy, so imagine the funeral first Plans are written from the inside: our team, our scenario, our enthusiasm. Kahneman calls the result the planning fallacy, forecasts hugging the best case instead of the track record of similar projects.
The receipts:
Scotland’s new parliament building: estimated at up to £40 million, finished at around £431 million. Rail projects worldwide: ridership overestimated by 106% on average, costs overrun by 45%. Home kitchen remodels: owners expected to pay about 18,658andpaidabout18,658 and paid about 18,658andpaidabout38,769. Two fixes:
The outside view. Ignore your story. Look up how similar projects actually went, and start your estimate there. The premortem (Klein’s idea). Before committing, gather the team and say: “Imagine it’s a year from now. We did this. It was a disaster. Write the history of why.” It works because it makes doubt socially safe. Once a group has decided, dissent starts to look like disloyalty. The premortem makes dissent the assignment. Steal this: run a ten-minute premortem on your next big decision. Then multiply your timeline by whatever similar projects actually took.
7. You’re two people, and the wrong one is running your life Kahneman splits you into an experiencing self (the one who feels each moment) and a remembering self (the one who keeps score afterward). They disagree, and the remembering self gets the vote.
In a colonoscopy study, patients reported their pain minute by minute. Afterward, they rated the whole ordeal, and their ratings ignored how long it lasted. What mattered was the worst moment and the final moment: the peak-end rule, plus duration neglect. A patient with an 8-minute procedure that ended painfully remembered it as worse than a patient whose procedure was three times longer but tapered off gently.
The same distortion shapes how we judge our lives. Kahneman’s focusing illusion: whatever you’re thinking about seems far more important than it really is. People assume sunny California must make you happier. It doesn’t, because Californians hardly think about the weather. The same trap makes us overestimate how much a new car, house, or gadget will improve our daily lives, and underrate things like friendships and hobbies that keep demanding our attention.
Steal this: end experiences well, because the ending is what gets remembered. And before a big purchase or move, ask: “How often will I actually be thinking about this?”
The honey If you only keep one thing:
Your mind is a story machine. It values coherence over completeness, ease over accuracy, and confidence over evidence.
You can’t switch that machine off, and Kahneman is clear that even he never fully escaped its tricks. But you can build around it:
Look for what’s missing. Name the real question. Distrust the feeling of certainty. Let simple formulas make the repeated calls. Check whether the environment lets anyone have real expertise. Run the premortem. Plan for the memory, and for the attention, not just the moment. The goal isn’t to stop having a gut. It’s to stop letting your gut cross-examine itself and rule that it’s innocent.
One honest caveat: some findings in the book, especially around social priming, have not held up well in replication, and I left those out on purpose. The ideas above rest on far firmer ground.
Source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).

summary: Your brain isn’t built to find the truth. It’s built to tell a good story, fast. Seven ideas from Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow on why confidence is a feeling, why a dumb formula beats the expert, and how to stop being the easiest person in the room to fool.
title: Your Gut Feeling Is a Con Artist (and You're the Mark)

I’m Otmane Echaibi, a systems hacker. I live in the terminal, and my home is the internet.
I write Python, Fish, Lua, Go, Rust and JavaScript, bash, sql. Each one has one job, and Python sits in the middle:
Outside the terminal I run marathons, write, and do math as an amateur.
I’m a minimalist, and it’s my philosophy, not a style. I keep my things few and my code small. The blog follows the same rule: say what’s needed, then stop.
What you’ll find here Notes on how things work: systems, code, math, and what long-distance running teaches about both. Math starts from the simplest case and builds up. I would rather leave something out than pad it.
Say hello Corrections, questions and arguments are welcome on the contact page.
